title: Cloud Network Segmentation
summary: Cloud network segmentation is the practice of dividing a cloud estate into virtual networks, subnets and rule sets so that traffic between workloads is explicitly permitted rather than implicitly allowed. The building blocks are provider constructs. A virtual network forms a routing boundary, subnets carve it into address ranges, security groups act as stateful per-interface firewalls attached to workloads, and network access control lists filter at the subnet edge. Private endpoints and private peering let services communicate without traversing the public internet, while egress rules and inspection appliances control outbound traffic, which matters because command-and-control callbacks and data exfiltration both travel outbound. Segmentation appears in landing zone design, in separating production from non-production, and in limiting the blast radius of a compromised workload. The mistake people make is assuming that a virtual network is closed by default: many environments allow broad east-west traffic inside it, so one stolen credential or one vulnerable service can reach everything the routing table permits.

beginner.definition: Network segmentation means splitting your computers into separate groups so that a problem in one group cannot easily reach another. In the cloud you build these groups with virtual networks and small rules called security groups. Each rule says which computers may talk to which, and on which port. Nothing should talk to anything else unless you allowed it on purpose.
beginner.whyItMatters: If every machine can reach every other machine, one stolen password can spread across your whole company. Attackers also move sideways from a weak test system into the systems that hold real customer data. Segmentation slows them down and gives your alarms time to fire. It also limits accidents, such as a broken script in one team deleting another team's database.
howItWorks: Divide your cloud estate into virtual networks, one for each environment such as production, test and development.
Split each network into subnets, and keep databases in subnets that have no direct route to the internet.
Attach security group rules to each machine, allowing only the ports and sources that the workload truly needs.
Use private endpoints so services talk to each other inside the provider network instead of over the public internet.
Control outgoing traffic too, because malware often needs to call home to receive commands.
Review the rules regularly and remove the temporary ones that nobody remembers adding.
beginner.example: Imagine a hospital with separate wards. A visitor can reach the front desk and the cafe, but not the operating theatres or the drug store. Each door needs a badge, and the badge only opens the rooms that belong to your job. If someone becomes ill in one ward, the hospital closes that ward and the rest keeps working. A cloud network works like this building. Subnets are the wards and security groups are the badge readers. Private endpoints are internal corridors that never open onto the street.
takeaways: Assume your cloud network is open until you add rules, because traffic between machines is often allowed by default.
Filter traffic in both directions, since blocking incoming connections alone does not stop a machine from calling out.
Keep production and test in separate networks, so a mistake or an attack in one cannot reach the other.

objectives: Explain what network segmentation is and why it limits the spread of an attack.
Describe the cloud building blocks used for segmentation, such as virtual networks, subnets and security groups.
Distinguish between controlling incoming traffic and controlling outgoing traffic.
Identify common segmentation mistakes, including overly broad rules and shared network accounts.
Describe how private connectivity reduces exposure to the public internet.
